home.title: Failure experiments
home.lead: Design any small system you like, break one part on purpose, and see what changes. Every run is reproducible from its file and seed.
home.emptyBody: Bring back the built-in examples, import a file, or start from a template.

starter.title: What do health checks actually save you?
starter.body: Two experiments that differ in exactly one setting. Server B crashes for 20 seconds while the client sends 100 requests per second. In the first, the load balancer never checks its backends. In the second, it probes them every 5 seconds and needs two failed probes, so it notices the crash after 5 to 10 seconds.
steps: Run the baseline and look at the failed requests.
Run the version with health checks.
Compare them and read why the numbers differ.
starter.note: In both, the crashed server refuses connections, so requests fail instantly and latency barely moves. For a failure that also makes clients wait, open the “Hanging backend” example.
starter.figure: Timeline: Server B is down from 20 to 40 seconds. Without health checks it receives traffic the whole time; with checks it is removed after about 5 seconds.

load-balanced.title: Load balancer

api-database.title: API and database
api-database.description: A two-hop chain: every API request calls the database.

cache-database.title: Cache in front of a database
cache-database.description: The API reads through a cache; misses go to the database.

worker-queue.title: Worker queue

microservices.title: Microservices
microservices.description: Load balancer, two APIs, a shared auth service and a shared database.

assumptions: Abstract request-level model: no TCP, TLS, packets or real HTTP proxy semantics.
Each component has fixed concurrency slots and a FIFO queue; there is no CPU, memory or GC model.
Health probes bypass the request queue and answer instantly when the component is up.
Components do not know when their caller gave up; they finish the work and the answer is discarded.
Numbers are scenario inputs, not measured performance of any product.

kindHints.service: slots, a queue, calls other components
kindHints.database: a service with a connection pool

node-failure.label: Component crash
node-failure.help: The component crashes at a given time. Work in progress is lost; when it recovers, its queue is empty.

slowdown.label: Slowdown
slowdown.help: The component's service time is multiplied by a factor and/or a fixed time is added for a window.

error-rate.label: Error rate
error-rate.help: A share of calls arriving at the component fail at once with an error, like a bug that hits only some requests.

capacity.label: Capacity drop
capacity.help: The component's concurrency drops to a number, for example half of its instances are gone.

link-latency.label: Link latency
link-latency.help: Extra one-way latency on a link, like a congested network.

link-loss.label: Link loss
link-loss.help: A share of calls over the link are lost: they never arrive and wait until the caller's timeout.

cache-flush.label: Cache flush
cache-flush.help: The cache answers nothing from memory during this window (a cold cache, a restart or a flush).

worker.capacity.label: Concurrency
worker.capacity.help: How many requests the component works on at the same time.

worker.queueCapacity.label: Queue size
worker.queueCapacity.help: Requests that may wait for a free slot. When the queue is full, new requests are rejected.

worker.serviceTimeMs.label: Service time
worker.serviceTimeMs.help: Time one request occupies a slot for the component's own work, not counting waits on other components. With an exponential distribution this is the mean.

worker.serviceTimeDistribution.label: Service time distribution
worker.serviceTimeDistribution.help: Fixed gives every request the same time. Exponential draws a random time per request from the seed.

queue.consumers.label: Workers
queue.consumers.help: How many jobs are processed at the same time.

queue.backlog.label: Backlog limit
queue.backlog.help: Jobs that may wait in the queue. When it is full, new requests are rejected.

cache.hitRatio.label: Hit ratio
cache.hitRatio.help: Share of lookups answered from memory without calling the component behind it.

balancer.algorithm.label: Algorithm
balancer.algorithm.help: How a backend is chosen. Round robin takes turns; least connections picks the one with the fewest open calls; random draws from the seed.

balancer.retries.label: Retry on another backend
balancer.retries.help: Extra attempts on another backend when a backend fails a call.

healthCheck.enabled.label: Health checks
healthCheck.enabled.help: When off, the load balancer keeps routing to every backend, even dead ones.

healthCheck.intervalMs.label: Probe interval
healthCheck.intervalMs.help: Time between probes to each backend. Longer intervals detect failures later.

healthCheck.probeTimeoutMs.label: Probe timeout
healthCheck.probeTimeoutMs.help: How long a probe to a hanging backend waits before counting as failed. Refused probes fail at once.

healthCheck.unhealthyThreshold.label: Unhealthy after
healthCheck.unhealthyThreshold.help: Consecutive failed probes before the backend is taken out of rotation.

healthCheck.healthyThreshold.label: Healthy after
healthCheck.healthyThreshold.help: Consecutive successful probes before a recovered backend gets traffic again.

link.latencyMs.label: Network latency
link.latencyMs.help: One-way latency added to every call and every answer over this link.

link.timeoutMs.label: Call timeout
link.timeoutMs.help: The caller gives up after this long and counts the call as failed. Leave empty to wait until the request deadline.

link.retries.label: Retries
link.retries.help: Extra attempts after a call over this link fails. Careful: retrying while the component behind it is sick can make things worse.

breaker.enabled.label: Circuit breaker
breaker.enabled.help: After a number of consecutive failures, calls are rejected immediately for a while, then one trial call is let through.

breaker.failureThreshold.label: Opens after
breaker.failureThreshold.help: Consecutive failed calls before the breaker opens.

breaker.openMs.label: Stays open for
breaker.openMs.help: How long the breaker rejects calls before letting one trial call through.

workload.arrival.label: Arrival pattern
workload.arrival.help: Constant sends requests at exact intervals. Poisson draws random gaps from the seed with the same average rate.

workload.offeredRps.label: Offered rate
workload.offeredRps.help: Requests the client sends per second, whether or not they succeed.

workload.startMs.label: Traffic starts at
workload.startMs.help: Simulated time when the client starts sending.

workload.durationMs.label: Traffic duration
workload.durationMs.help: How long the client keeps sending at this rate.

workload.timeoutMs.label: Client timeout
workload.timeoutMs.help: A request without a response after this long counts as failed. A response arriving later is discarded.

burst.atMs.label: Burst starts at
burst.atMs.help: Simulated time the extra traffic begins.

burst.durationMs.label: Burst length
burst.durationMs.help: How long the extra traffic lasts.

burst.extraRps.label: Extra rate
burst.extraRps.help: Added on top of the base rate during the burst.

fault.recoverAtMs.label: Recovers at
fault.recoverAtMs.help: Simulated time the component comes back with an empty queue. Leave empty to keep it down.

fault.untilMs.label: Ends at
fault.untilMs.help: Simulated time the fault stops. Leave empty to keep it until the end.

fault.behavior.label: Failure behavior
fault.behavior.help: Refuse: connections are rejected at once (process crashed). Hang: no answer until the caller gives up (host unreachable).

fault.factor.label: Slowdown factor
fault.factor.help: Service time is multiplied by this. 1 means unchanged.

fault.addMs.label: Added time
fault.addMs.help: Fixed milliseconds added to every call.

fault.rate.label: Share
fault.rate.help: Share of calls affected, drawn from the seed.

fault.capacity.label: Capacity during the fault
fault.capacity.help: The component's concurrency during the fault window.

run.seed.label: Seed
run.seed.help: Same seed, same inputs and same engine version always give identical results.

run.horizonMs.label: Horizon
run.horizonMs.help: Simulated time the run stops. Auto: end of traffic plus one client timeout.

run.sampleWindowMs.label: Chart window
run.sampleWindowMs.help: Width of the time buckets used for charts. Does not change the simulation.

inspector.settingsDescription: Change the components, traffic, faults and notes of the experiment.
inspector.pickComponent: Select a component on the canvas, or pick one here, to see and change its settings.
inspector.addDownstream: Add a component called from here
inspector.linksHint: Links follow the direction of calls: the client calls the first component, and every component calls everything behind it in order.
inspector.name: Name
inspector.nameHelp: Display name only. The id {{id}} is what faults and exports refer to.
inspector.noIncoming: Nothing calls this component yet, so it will never receive traffic. Connect it from another component.
inspector.removedWithFaults_one: Also removed {{count}} fault that targeted it. Undo with Ctrl+Z.
inspector.removedWithFaults_other: Also removed {{count}} faults that targeted it. Undo with Ctrl+Z.
inspector.needOneComponent: An experiment needs at least one component besides the client.
inspector.clientSummary: The client sends {{rps}} req/s for {{duration}} and gives up after {{timeout}}.
inspector.detectionHint: Expected detection delay. A component that refuses connections is noticed {{min}} to {{max}} after it crashes, depending on where in the probe cycle the crash lands. A hanging component takes up to {{probeTimeout}} longer, because each probe waits for its timeout.
inspector.noDetectionHint: Without health checks the load balancer cannot notice a dead backend. Every request it sends there fails until the component comes back.
inspector.capacityHint: At most about {{rps}} req/s ({{slots}} slots ÷ {{time}}{{avg}}). More than that and the queue grows.
inspector.queueCapacityHint: Workers finish about {{rps}} jobs/s ({{slots}} workers ÷ {{time}}{{avg}}). More than that and the backlog grows.
inspector.linkHint: These settings apply to every call from the first component to the second.
inspector.retriesNoTimeout: Retries without a timeout only kick in when a call fails immediately. To retry slow calls, add a timeout.
inspector.entryCapacityHint: {{name}} can handle about {{rps}} req/s, so steady traffic uses {{load}}% of its capacity.
inspector.burstsHelp: Extra traffic on top of the steady rate for a while.
inspector.faultsIntro: A fault changes how one component or link behaves at a given time. Pick a kind, then a target.
inspector.noFaults: No faults. Without one, this experiment is a healthy reference run.
inspector.noTargetForKind: There is no component or link this fault kind can target yet.
inspector.seedHint: The seed only matters for the random parts: Poisson arrivals, exponential service times, caches, random routing and share-based faults. Without those, every seed gives the same result.

notes.title: Title
notes.question: Question
notes.questionHelp: The one thing this experiment should answer.
notes.expectedHelp: Teaching hypotheses, one per line. They are shown next to results but never computed or checked automatically.
notes.assumptionsHelp: Simplifications this model makes, one per line. They are exported with every result.
notes.idHelp: Exports are named {{id}}.experiment.json. Faults and comparisons refer to it, so rename before sharing.

results.heading: Results
results.errorHint: Your settings are unchanged. Fix the input or try again.
results.noneBody: Run the experiment to see what happens to every request: a timeline of successes and failures, latency, queues, and an explanation built from the simulated events. It takes about a second and runs in your browser.
results.staleBody: The results below still show the previous settings.

summary.p95Help: p95 means 95 of every 100 requests took this long or less.
summary.onTick: (crash hit a probe, the shortest case)
summary.inFlightSome: no outcome at {{at}}; not counted as success or failure

charts.requestsSub: Counted per {{window}} ms window by when they ended (offered: by arrival)
charts.latencySub: Nearest-rank percentiles of requests that ended in each window. Timeouts count as the full timeout.
charts.callsSub: Calls arriving at each component, retries included
charts.queueSub: Peak requests waiting per window, by component
charts.busySub: Peak slots in use per window, by component

legend.gap: Down, but the load balancer still sends it requests
legend.cursor: Replay position (click a chart to move it)

perNode.title: Per component
perNode.note: “Failed here” counts requests whose failure originated at that component. “Slots busy” is busy slot-time over the whole run.

explain.title: What happened
explain.intro: Generated from this run's events and counts. It describes what the model did, not why a real system would.
explain.expectedIntro: Written with the experiment as hypotheses. Check them against the results yourself; they are not evaluated automatically.
explain.noExpected: None written. Add some in the Notes tab.

outcome.title: {{successPct}}% of requests succeeded
outcome.body: {{succeeded}} of {{offered}} offered requests succeeded and {{failed}} failed.
outcome.body_inflight: {{succeeded}} of {{offered}} offered requests succeeded and {{failed}} failed; {{inFlight}} were still in flight when the run stopped at {{measuredMs}}.

origin.title: Failures mostly originated at {{node}}
origin.body: {{count}} of all failed requests ({{pct}}%) first went wrong at {{node}}: that is where they were refused, timed out or lost, even though the client saw them as errors from the component in front of it.
origin.body_reason: {{count}} of all failed requests ({{pct}}%) first went wrong at {{node}}, mostly as {{reason}} ({{reasonCount}}). The components in front of it only passed the failure on.

crashDetected.title: {{node}} crashed at {{atMs}}
crashDetected.body_tick: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}. The load balancer marked it unhealthy at {{detectedAtMs}}, {{delayMs}} after the crash. That is the shortest delay these settings allow, because the crash landed exactly on a probe; a crash just after a probe would take up to {{maxMs}}. {{lost}} requests failed because they were lost in the crash or sent there before the failure was noticed.
crashDetected.body_range: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}. The load balancer marked it unhealthy at {{detectedAtMs}}, {{delayMs}} after the crash. With these settings detection takes between {{minMs}} and {{maxMs}}, depending on where in the probe cycle the crash lands. {{lost}} requests failed because they were lost in the crash or sent there before the failure was noticed.
crashDetected.body_tick_restored: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}. The load balancer marked it unhealthy at {{detectedAtMs}}, {{delayMs}} after the crash, the shortest delay possible because the crash landed exactly on a probe; a crash just after a probe would take up to {{maxMs}}. {{lost}} requests failed before that was noticed. It recovered at {{recoveredAtMs}} and got traffic again at {{restoredAtMs}}, {{restoreDelayMs}} after recovering.
crashDetected.body_range_restored: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}. The load balancer marked it unhealthy at {{detectedAtMs}}, {{delayMs}} after the crash; with these settings detection takes {{minMs}} to {{maxMs}}. {{lost}} requests failed before that was noticed. It recovered at {{recoveredAtMs}} and got traffic again at {{restoredAtMs}}, {{restoreDelayMs}} after recovering.
crashDetected.body_tick_notRestored: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}. The load balancer marked it unhealthy at {{detectedAtMs}}, {{delayMs}} after the crash (the fastest case; up to {{maxMs}} is possible). {{lost}} requests failed before that was noticed. It recovered at {{recoveredAtMs}} but had not been put back into rotation when the run ended.
crashDetected.body_range_notRestored: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}. The load balancer marked it unhealthy at {{detectedAtMs}}, {{delayMs}} after the crash ({{minMs}} to {{maxMs}} is possible). {{lost}} requests failed before that was noticed. It recovered at {{recoveredAtMs}} but had not been put back into rotation when the run ended.

crashRecoveredFirst.title: {{node}} crashed at {{atMs}}
crashRecoveredFirst.body: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}, and recovered at {{recoveredAtMs}} before the health checks noticed. {{lost}} requests failed meanwhile.

crashNeverDetected.title: {{node}} crashed at {{atMs}}
crashNeverDetected.body: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}. The health checks never marked it unhealthy before the run ended. {{lost}} requests failed because of it.

crashUnwatched.title: {{node}} crashed at {{atMs}}
crashUnwatched.body_recovered: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}. No health check watches it, so traffic kept going there until it recovered at {{recoveredAtMs}}. {{lost}} requests failed because they were lost in the crash or sent there while it was down.
crashUnwatched.body_down: {{node}} went down at {{atMs}}, {{behavior}}. No health check watches it, so traffic kept going there for the rest of the run. {{lost}} requests failed because they were lost in the crash or sent there while it was down.

slowdown.title: {{target}} slowed down at {{atMs}}
slowdown.body: From {{atMs}} to {{untilMs}} {{target}}'s service time was longer than usual. Every component calling it held its slot longer, so queues in front of it grew too.

error-rate.title: {{target}} returned errors from {{atMs}}
error-rate.body: From {{atMs}} to {{untilMs}} a share of calls to {{target}} failed at once. Its callers gave up or retried, depending on their link settings.

capacity.title: {{target}} lost capacity at {{atMs}}
capacity.body: From {{atMs}} to {{untilMs}} {{target}} had fewer slots. Work in progress finished; new work queued or was rejected.

link-latency.title: Link {{target}} slowed down at {{atMs}}
link-latency.body: From {{atMs}} to {{untilMs}} every call and answer over {{target}} carried extra latency.

link-loss.title: Link {{target}} lost calls from {{atMs}}
link-loss.body: From {{atMs}} to {{untilMs}} a share of calls over {{target}} never arrived. Callers only found out when their timeout ran out.

cache-flush.title: {{target}} was flushed at {{atMs}}
cache-flush.body: From {{atMs}} to {{untilMs}} {{target}} answered nothing from memory, so every lookup fell through to the component behind it.

saturated.title: {{node}} ran out of room
saturated.body: {{node}}'s queue reached its limit of {{queueCapacity}} requests. Its slots were busy {{utilizationPct}}% of the run.
saturated.body_rejected: {{node}}'s queue reached its limit of {{queueCapacity}} requests and {{rejected}} requests were rejected. Its slots were busy {{utilizationPct}}% of the run.

nearlySaturated.title: {{node}} was nearly saturated
nearlySaturated.body: {{node}}'s slots were busy {{utilizationPct}}% of the run; peak queue {{peakQueue}} of {{queueCapacity}}.

cache.title: {{node}} answered {{hitPct}}% from memory
cache.body: Of {{lookups}} lookups, {{hitPct}}% were answered without calling the component behind it. The rest fell through.

queue.title: {{node}} processed {{done}} jobs
queue.body: {{done}} jobs finished and {{failed}} failed. The backlog peaked at {{peakBacklog}}; jobs waited {{meanWaitMs}} on average and {{maxWaitMs}} at most, although their clients were answered at once.

retries.title: Retries multiplied the calls to {{target}}
retries.body: Of {{calls}} calls to {{target}}, {{retries}} ({{pct}}%) were retries. While the component behind is slow, retries add load exactly when it can least cope.

breaker.title: The circuit breaker {{source}} → {{target}} opened {{opens}} times
breaker.body: While open, {{rejected}} calls were rejected at once without waiting. That fails requests faster, but frees {{source}}'s slots and protects {{target}}.

latencyFailuresSlow.title: Failed requests made clients wait longest
latencyFailuresSlow.body: Successful requests took {{p50Ms}} at the median and {{p95Ms}} at p95 (n = {{n}}). Counting every request that ended, failures included, p95 is {{endedP95Ms}} (n = {{endedN}}): a timed-out client waits the full timeout before it learns the request failed.

latencyTail.title: Latency has a long tail
latencyTail.body: Successful requests took {{p50Ms}} at the median and {{p95Ms}} at p95 (n = {{n}}). The gap comes from time spent waiting in queues.

latencyFlat.title: Successful requests were consistently fast
latencyFlat.body: Successful requests took {{p50Ms}} at the median and {{p95Ms}} at p95 (n = {{n}}).

probes.title: The load balancer sent {{probes}} health probes
probes.body: In this model probes are free: they skip the queue and use no capacity, so a shorter probe interval only shows its benefit. Real probes cost a little server and network time.

late.title: {{late}} responses arrived too late
late.body: Components finished {{late}} pieces of work after their caller had given up. That work used capacity but counts only as a failure.

eventLimit.title: The run stopped early
eventLimit.body: The run hit the event limit at {{measuredMs}}. Results cover only that part; shorten the traffic or lower the rate.

no-healthy-backend.label: No healthy backend
no-healthy-backend.description: The load balancer had no backend marked healthy to send the request to.

refused.label: Refused
refused.description: The call was sent to a component that had crashed and refuses connections.

queue-full.label: Queue full
queue-full.description: Every slot was busy and the queue had no room left.

lost-in-crash.label: Lost in crash
lost-in-crash.description: The request was being served or waiting in a queue when its component crashed.

timeout.label: Timed out
timeout.description: No response arrived before the client deadline or the call timeout.

circuit-open.label: Breaker open
circuit-open.description: The circuit breaker was open and rejected the call at once.

injected-error.label: Error
injected-error.description: The component returned an error because of an error-rate fault.

events.truncated: This run produced more request events than the table keeps. State changes are complete; later request-level events are not listed. Metrics are not affected.
events.noEvents: No events of this kind in this run.
events.jump: Move the replay to this moment
events.ordering: Times are simulated. Events at the same instant are listed in the engine's fixed order: faults, probe results, transfers, completions, timeouts, then arrivals.

checks.title: Model checks: {{passed}} of {{total}} passed
checks.intro: Checked independently from the event stream after every run. A failure here means a bug in the engine, not in your experiment.

items.queue-bounds: Queues stay between 0 and their size

checks.reproIntro: Same settings, seed and engine version give the identical event trace on any machine. To check a copy, compare the behavior digest (it ignores ids, titles and notes) and the trace fingerprint. The file digest also covers names and notes, so it changes when a copy is renamed.
checks.tookValue: {{ms}} ms of wall-clock time (not part of the result)
checks.identical: Identical. The second run produced trace {{digest}} and the same metrics.
checks.different: Different result ({{digest}}). This is a determinism bug; please report it with the exported experiment.

verify.title: Result file check
verify.rerunning: Re-running the experiment from {{source}} to check its results…
verify.stale: The settings were changed after import, so these results can no longer be checked against {{source}}.
verify.nothingToCheck: {{source}} has no digests to check against.
verify.engineDiffers: The file was produced by engine {{file}}; this is engine {{here}}. Different engine versions may legitimately give different traces.

rows.failed-wait: Client time spent on failed requests

compare.title: Compare two experiments
compare.lead: Pick a baseline (A) and a variant (B). A comparison teaches the most when exactly one behavior setting differs between them.
compare.missing: One of the experiments in this link is not in this browser. Choose another one above.
compare.pickTwo: Choose two experiments above. Both run automatically in your browser.
compare.whatChanged: What changed from A to B
compare.oneChange: Exactly one behavior setting differs, so differences in the results can be attributed to it within this model.
compare.noChange: No behavior setting differs. The results will be identical, which makes this a reproducibility check.
compare.manyChanges: {{count}} behavior settings differ. A difference in the results cannot be attributed to any single one of them. For a clean comparison, create a variant and change only one thing.
compare.ignored: Titles, notes, names and canvas positions are ignored: they never affect results.
compare.invalid: “{{title}}” has settings that need fixing before it can run. Open it to see the problems.

caution.fewerSuccesses: B has fewer successful requests. Failed requests are not in this number, so the remaining successes can look faster without anything improving.
caution.moreSuccesses: B completes requests that failed in A. Those extra successes can be slower, so a higher value here is not necessarily worse.

compare.percentileNote: p50, p95 and p99: half, 95 and 99 of every 100 requests took this long or less. “Successful” rows leave failed requests out; “all ended” rows include them, with a timeout counted as the full timeout.

charts.endedP95Sub: Includes failures; a timed-out request counts as the full timeout

compare.differentWindows: The two experiments use different chart windows, so their timelines are not overlaid. Set the same chart window in both (Run tab) to compare them over time.
caveats: Both runs come from the same abstract request-level model. They compare designs inside the model, not real products.
A difference is only attributable to a setting when that setting is the only one that changed.
Detection depends on where in the probe cycle a crash lands. A crash exactly on a probe is the fastest case; move the failure time to see the slower ones.
With random traffic or service times, a single seed is one sample. Use the seed check above.
Assumptions for each experiment are listed in its “What happened” tab and in every export.
compare.reproduceHint: Import the .comparison.json file into FaultWorks, or each side's experiment, and run it. The run must reproduce these fingerprints:

narrative.failed: Failed requests went from {{a}} in A to {{b}} in B{{pct}}.
narrative.hiddenWait: Latency percentiles are the same in A and B, yet clients spent {{a}} waiting on failed requests in A and {{b}} in B. Percentiles hide this: once more than 5% of requests time out in both runs, p95 is simply the timeout in both.
narrative.fastFailures: Latency did not change. The failures were rejected immediately (refused, no room, breaker or error), so they added almost no waiting time, and the requests that succeeded were served the same way. A backend that hangs instead of refusing does change latency: try the “Hanging backend” example.
narrative.sameLatency: Latency percentiles are the same in A and B.
narrative.p95: p95 latency of successful requests went from {{a}} in A to {{b}} in B.
narrative.calls: Calls between components went from {{a}} in A to {{b}} in B; retries or breakers changed how much work reached the components behind.
narrative.detection: The first failure was detected {{a}} in A and {{b}} in B.

sweep.title: Is it the seed?
sweep.deterministic: Both experiments use constant traffic and nothing random, so the seed has no effect: every seed gives exactly the same numbers. The difference above comes entirely from the settings.
sweep.intro: At least one experiment has random parts, so a single run is one sample. Repeat both with the same {{n}} seeds ({{from}}–{{to}}) to see the spread.
sweep.caption: Results across {{n}} seeds
sweep.note: Seeds are paired: run i of A and run i of B use the same seed. Ten runs show the spread; they are not enough for confidence intervals.

import.title: Import
import.description: Choose a FaultWorks .json file or paste its contents: an experiment, a result (it is re-run and checked) or a comparison (both sides come in). Files are checked against the schema and stay in this browser.
import.failed_one: This experiment can't be imported yet ({{count}} problem)
import.failed_other: This experiment can't be imported yet ({{count}} problems)
import.reused: “{{title}}” is already in this browser with the same settings, so the existing copy is used.
import.renamed: A different experiment already uses the id {{from}}, so this one is saved as {{id}} and marked “(imported)”.
import.resultDone: Imported the experiment inside the result file “{{title}}”

error.title: Something broke on this page

limitations.abstract: Abstract request-level discrete-event simulation; not packet-level networking or a model of any specific proxy.
limitations.singleSeed: A single seed is a deterministic demonstration, not statistical evidence.
limitations.notMeasurement: Simulated metrics are model outputs, not measurements of a real system.

validation.id: Use 1–48 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, starting with a letter or digit.
validation.title: Give the experiment a title.

graph.duplicateNodeId: Two components use the id “{{id}}”. Ids must be unique.
graph.oneClient: An experiment needs exactly one client; this one has {{count}}.
graph.danglingLink: The link {{source}} → {{target}} points to a component that does not exist.
graph.intoClient: {{source}} calls the client. The client only sends; it is never called.
graph.balancerToBalancer: Load balancer {{source}} calls load balancer {{target}}. Put a component between them or connect the backends directly.
graph.clientOneLink: The client must call exactly one component; it calls {{count}}.
graph.balancerNeedsBackend: Load balancer {{node}} has no backends. Connect it to at least one component.
graph.cacheOneDownstream: Cache {{node}} can only call one component behind it.
graph.unreachable: Nothing calls {{node}}, so it would never receive traffic. Connect it or remove it.
graph.cycle: Calls go in a circle: {{cycle}}. A request must never be able to call itself.

guide.title: Model guide
guide.lead: FaultWorks runs an abstract, request-level discrete-event simulation. This page says exactly what that model does, so you can judge what a result does and does not tell you.

sections.limits: Limits and what is not modeled

what: An experiment is a directed graph: one client and up to 11 other components, connected by links that follow the direction of calls. The client calls one component; a load balancer forwards to one of its backends; services, databases and caches do their own work and then call every component behind them in order; a worker queue answers at once and does the work later.
Time is simulated in whole microseconds and moves from event to event; nothing depends on how fast your computer is or how fast the replay plays.

components.client: Sends requests at a constant rate (exact intervals) or as a Poisson process (random gaps from the seed), plus optional bursts. Each request has a deadline: the client timeout.
components.load-balancer: Picks a backend by round robin, least connections or at random among the backends it considers healthy. Without health checks it considers every backend healthy forever. It can retry on another backend when a backend fails a call.
components.service: Has a number of slots (concurrency) and a FIFO queue. A call occupies a slot for its own service time plus all the time spent waiting on the components behind it.
components.database: Behaves like a service; its slots stand for a connection pool. Kept separate only so your design reads well.
components.cache: Answers a share of lookups from memory according to its hit ratio (drawn from the seed). Misses fall through to the single component behind it.
components.queue: Stores work and answers the caller at once (or rejects it when the backlog is full). A number of workers process the backlog, call the components behind it, and their outcomes are recorded as jobs, not requests.

steps: The request reaches the first component over the client's link. If the link has latency, the trip takes time.
A load balancer picks a backend. If none is marked healthy, the request fails at once (no healthy backend).
If the component has crashed with the refuse behavior, the call fails at once (refused). With hang, it waits until the caller's timeout.
If a slot is free the work starts; otherwise the call queues; if the queue is full it fails (queue full).
After its own work, the component calls every component behind it in order while still holding its slot. A failure anywhere in the chain fails that call, unless the link retries.

The request succeeds when its answer reaches the client at or before the deadline. Otherwise it fails with a timeout. Components do not know the client gave up: the work finishes later and the answer is discarded.
note: Every request ends exactly once. Events at the same instant are processed in a fixed order: faults, probe results, transfers over links, completions, timeouts, probe sends, arrivals. An answer landing exactly on the deadline counts as on time.

intro: A fault changes how one component or link behaves during a window. Seven kinds are available, and several faults may be active at once.
health: With health checks on, the load balancer probes every backend each interval, starting at time 0. Probes bypass the request queue and answer instantly from a running component. After the configured number of consecutive failed probes the backend is removed from rotation; after the configured number of successes it is added back. Probes are free in the model: they use no capacity, so a very short interval shows only its benefit. This is a simplified active check; it does not reproduce any specific proxy.
The period between a crash and its detection is the amber hatched band on every timeline: the component is down, but still receives traffic.

resilience: Every link can have a call timeout, retries and a circuit breaker. A timeout makes the caller give up and free its slot; the work at the called component continues and its answer is discarded as a late response.
Retries happen immediately, without backoff, to the same component. While that component is slow, every client request can become several calls: that is a retry storm.

A circuit breaker counts consecutive failures over a link. At the threshold it opens and rejects calls at once for a while. Then one trial call is let through: success closes the breaker, failure opens it again.

offered.def: Requests the client generated, whether or not they succeeded.

succeeded.def: Requests whose answer arrived at or before their deadline.

failed.def: Requests that ended without success, broken down by reason and by the component where the failure originated.

inFlight.def: Requests without an outcome when the run stopped. Counted neither as success nor failure. Offered = succeeded + failed + still in flight.

latency.def: Completion time minus arrival time. “Successful” latency leaves failed requests out. “All ended” latency includes them, with a timeout counted as the full timeout and a refusal as almost zero, so fast failures can make it look better.

percentiles.def: p95 is the time within which 95 of every 100 requests finished; p50 is the median. The nearest-rank method is used, so the value is always a real sample, and the number of samples (n) is always shown.

endedLatency.def: Time from sending a call to receiving its answer, measured at the caller, including the components behind it.

failedWait.term: Client time spent on failed requests
failedWait.def: Total time clients waited on requests that eventually failed. Percentiles cannot show this once more than 5% of requests fail.

calls.def: Every attempt over a link. Retries count as extra calls, so calls can far exceed requests.

detection.def: Time the load balancer marked a component unhealthy minus the time it actually crashed.

queue.def: Peak value within each chart window, per component. For a worker queue, the backlog is the jobs waiting for a worker.

reproducibility: The same experiment, seed and engine version produce the same event trace, byte for byte. Random numbers come from a seeded SFC32 generator with separate streams for arrivals, each component, each load balancer and each link, so adding a component does not change the random numbers another one sees.
Every result carries a behavior digest (SHA-256 of the settings that affect results) and a fingerprint of the full trace. The Engine checks tab can re-run an experiment and compare both.
A single seed is a deterministic demonstration, not statistical evidence. When an experiment has random parts, the Compare page can repeat both sides with ten paired seeds.

intro: After every run, the event stream is checked independently of the engine's own bookkeeping:
items: every request is accounted for (offered = succeeded + failed + in flight);
each request ends exactly once, and late responses only follow a caller giving up;
queues stay between zero and their size;
note: The engine itself is covered by reference cases with hand-computed answers and by property-based tests over hundreds of random experiments on every test run.

items: No TCP, TLS, packets, connection pooling, keep-alive or DNS.
No retry backoff, rate limiting, bulkheads or autoscaling.
No CPU, memory, garbage collection or operating-system scheduling.
No claim of parity with NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, Kafka or any product.
limits.budget: Runs are limited to {{minutes}} minutes of simulated time, about {{requests}} offered requests and {{nodes}} components, so a browser tab never locks up.
note: Use the results to understand and discuss failure dynamics. Do not use them as capacity plans, SLA estimates or predictions of production behavior.
